q: A nightly job must classify 80,000 records. Results are reviewed the next business morning. Cost is the main concern. Which approach fits?
o: Synchronous Messages API calls issued in parallel
The Message Batches API, which processes asynchronous workloads at reduced cost
Streaming requests to reduce total wall-clock time
Reducing max_tokens on synchronous calls
e: Nothing consumes results until morning, the signal for batch and its 50% discount. Parallel synchronous calls don't lower per-token cost, streaming optimizes a dimension nobody measures here, and trimming max_tokens ignores the realtime-versus-batch tradeoff.

q: A requirement states customer records must be processed within the EU. Which infrastructure decision follows most directly?
o: Use a regional endpoint that guarantees geographic routing
Use a global endpoint for maximum availability
Encrypt the payload before sending it
Reduce the retention period on application logs
e: Residency is met by regional endpoints with guaranteed geographic routing. Global endpoints route dynamically for availability, the opposite of what residency requires. Encryption and log retention are good practice but don't control where processing happens.

q: An enterprise requires every production model version change to be recorded, reviewed, and approved before release. Which framework does this requirement come from?
o: Agile, which mandates sprint review of all changes
ITIL-style service management, where change and release management govern production changes
Waterfall, which requires phase gate sign-off
DevOps, which automates approvals away
e: Change records, approval boards, and release management are service management concepts, and a model version change is a production change like any other. Agile and Waterfall describe how work is planned and delivered rather than how production change is governed.

q: Why can a Claude feature not rely solely on exact-match regression tests?
o: The API response format changes frequently
Model output is non-deterministic, so correctness must be graded against criteria
Tests cannot make network calls
Token counts vary between runs
e: Non-determinism means the same prompt can produce different valid outputs, so evals grade against criteria rather than asserting string equality. Deterministic code around the model is still unit tested normally.

q: A request fails with a 400 invalid_request_error. The messages array begins with an entry whose role is 'system'. What is the fix?
o: Move the system entry to the end of the messages array
Pass the content in the top-level system parameter instead
Change its role to 'assistant'
Add a cache_control block to the entry
e: The Messages API takes system as a top-level parameter; there is no system role inside messages. Reordering an invalid role doesn't make it valid, and cache_control is unrelated to request schema.

q: A batch of 5,000 classifications completes with no errors, but labels are mismatched to records. The pipeline zips results positionally against the input list. What is wrong?
o: Batch requests silently use a smaller model
Batch results return in nondeterministic order and must be joined on custom_id
Prompt caching returned another request's cached output
The batch exceeded its window and returned partial results
e: Batch requests process concurrently and results are not guaranteed to return in submission order, so custom_id is the join key. Caching never returns another request's output, and batch honors the model parameter.

q: After a release added a current timestamp to the top of a cached system prompt, cache_read_input_tokens dropped to near zero. Why?
o: The prompt now exceeds the maximum cacheable length
The cached prefix differs on every request, so no two requests share a prefix
The 5-minute TTL stops refreshing when a prompt contains variables
Timestamps are explicitly excluded from cacheable content
e: Prompt caching requires an exact prefix match. A value that changes every request, placed at the top of the prefix, means every call is a cache write and never a read. The fix is placement, not TTL.

q: A streaming endpoint logs HTTP 200 for every upstream call, yet users report answers stopping mid-sentence with no error shown. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The client disconnected and the server did not notice
An error event arrived in the stream after the 200 status was committed
The stream buffered incorrectly and dropped the final chunk
The model returned stop_reason end_turn prematurely
e: Because the HTTP status is sent before generation finishes, streaming responses can carry error events after a 200. A streaming client needs the same error branching as a non-streaming one, plus a policy for partial output already shown.

q: A pipeline analyzes 60-page contracts including tables and signature blocks. The team currently runs a separate OCR step and sends extracted plain text. What does sending the PDF as a document block change?
o: Nothing, since PDF support performs the same text extraction internally
Pages are processed visually as well as textually, so charts, tables, and layout survive without separate OCR
PDFs bypass token costs because they are treated as attachments
The document must first be converted to .docx for full support
e: PDF support runs through vision: pages are rendered as images alongside extracted text, so visual structure is preserved. Budget roughly 1,500 to 3,000 tokens per page. Office formats like .docx are the ones needing conversion, not PDFs.

q: A legal team queries the same 90-page contract dozens of times a day. Requests are large and slow. Which change most directly addresses this?
o: Upload the document once via the Files API and reference it by file_id
Split the contract across several parallel synchronous requests
Convert the PDF to plain text to remove image token costs
Raise max_tokens so the whole document fits in one response
e: The Files API lets you upload once and reference by file_id across requests, keeping payloads small instead of re-sending the document every time. Converting to text discards the visual structure contract review depends on, and max_tokens governs output rather than input.

q: An application answers questions from supplied source documents, and reviewers must verify each answer against the original text. Which feature addresses this most directly?
o: Extended thinking, so reviewers can read the model's reasoning
Citations enabled on the document block, referencing the exact source passages
A higher effort level to improve accuracy
Structured outputs with a confidence score field
e: Citations grounds responses in supplied documents with references to the specific passages used, which is what verification requires. Thinking shows reasoning rather than sourcing, effort doesn't create traceability, and a self-reported confidence score is not evidence.

q: An enterprise has an existing AWS commitment and wants Claude billed through it. What is the most relevant integration consideration?
o: Claude is unavailable outside the first-party API
Model identifiers and feature availability can differ, and authentication uses the cloud provider's IAM
The Messages API request format is entirely different on cloud platforms
Prompt caching cannot be used through cloud vendors
e: Claude runs on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. The practical differences are model ID conventions, lag in feature and beta availability, endpoint types, and provider IAM in place of an Anthropic API key.

q: A service fans out 300 concurrent Claude requests when a job starts and immediately receives 429s. What is the correct change?
o: Wrap each call in a retry loop with a fixed short delay
Limit concurrency with a queue or semaphore and ramp traffic gradually
Switch to a larger model, which has higher rate limits
Disable streaming to close connections faster
e: Rate limits are per-organization and sharp ramps can trip acceleration limits, so shaping concurrency is the fix. A fixed-delay retry loop increases volume at the worst moment and ignores retry-after. Model tier does not determine rate limits.

q: A team hand-rolls a retry decorator around every call made through the official SDK. What is the concern?
o: The SDK does not support retries, so this is necessary
The SDK already retries transient failures with backoff and honors retry-after, so a second layer multiplies request volume
Retries are prohibited by the API terms
Retry logic belongs in the model configuration
e: Official SDKs retry connection errors, 408, 409, 429, and 5xx twice by default with exponential backoff, honoring retry-after, and the count is configurable. Layering a custom fixed-delay retry compounds load during exactly the incident it should survive.

q: A team is using Claude Code to migrate a large legacy module to a new framework. Which practice most reduces risk?
o: Complete the migration in one large change so the codebase is never in a mixed state
Work in bounded increments with tests passing between each, and avoid adding behavior in the same change
Skip code review for AI-generated changes since the model follows existing patterns
Refactor and add the new features together to avoid touching files twice
e: Incremental refactoring with green tests between steps makes large-scale migration safe, and separating refactoring from behavior change keeps failures attributable. AI-generated code needs the same review rigor as human-written code.

q: A team wants a coding standard applied automatically in every Claude Code session in a repository, without anyone re-typing it. Where should it live?
o: In the first message of each session
In the project's CLAUDE.md, committed to version control
In a user's personal notes outside the repository
In the description of each custom tool
e: CLAUDE.md loads automatically and, when committed, applies for everyone on the project. Choose the instruction surface matching the durability required; a typed message lasts one session.

q: An application summarizes documents uploaded by end users. Where should the uploaded content be placed?
o: Concatenated into the system prompt so Claude treats it as authoritative
In a user turn, clearly delimited and separated from trusted instructions
In the tool description so it is available to every tool
Split evenly between the system prompt and the user turn
e: Untrusted content must stay structurally separate from trusted instructions and be clearly delimited. Placing user content in the system prompt collapses the trust boundary and breaks prompt caching.

q: An extraction schema requires a contract_end_date field. Some contracts genuinely have none, and the model fabricates dates for those. What schema change helps most?
o: Add an instruction telling the model not to guess
Make the field explicitly nullable so declining is representable in the schema
Change the field type from date to string
Mark the field required so the model pays more attention to it
e: If the schema cannot express 'not present', the model must produce something. Making it nullable gives a valid way to decline. Marking it required makes fabrication more likely, not less.

q: A long Claude Code session began with a database migration and has drifted into unrelated frontend work. Quality has declined. What is the best practice?
o: Increase the model's effort level to compensate
Start a fresh session for the new task rather than carrying unrelated context
Add a message restating that the earlier task is complete
Switch to a model with a larger context window
e: Session hygiene means starting fresh at task boundaries. Carrying unrelated context degrades quality, wastes tokens, and risks contradictory instructions. A larger window delays the problem without solving it.

q: A team has installed eleven plugins across their Claude Code projects, several with overlapping capabilities. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Sessions will fail to start because of a plugin limit
More tokens spent on tool definitions per request and greater ambiguity when selecting a tool
Plugins will automatically deduplicate their overlapping tools
Prompt caching will be disabled
e: Every installed plugin expands the tool surface, costing tokens on every request and increasing the chance the model picks the wrong tool. Plugins should be managed as dependencies and installed deliberately.

q: A production service's output quality drops on a day with no deploy and no prompt change. The model is specified by an alias. What is the remediation?
o: Add post-processing to restore the previous output shape
Pin an explicit dated model identifier and gate future upgrades on an eval re-run
Lower the temperature to stabilize the output
Move the alias into an environment variable
e: An unpinned alias lets the underlying model change without a deploy, matching quality shifting on a day nothing shipped. Moving the alias to an environment variable relocates the config without stopping the drift.

q: Which file should be committed so a team shares the same Claude Code permission rules and hooks?
o: .claude/settings.local.json
.claude/settings.json
A .env file in the repository root
The user-level ~/.claude/settings.json
e: Project settings.json is the shared, committed configuration. The .local.json variant is personal and gitignored, user-level settings apply to one developer, and secrets never belong in a committed file.

q: How should prompts be managed in a production Claude application?
o: Embedded as string literals near the code that uses them, for locality
Versioned in source control with review, tied to eval results, and rollback-capable
Stored in a database and edited directly in production for fast iteration
Regenerated by the model at deploy time to stay current
e: Prompts are code. Version them, review them, tie each version to eval results, and make rollback as fast as a code rollback. Editing directly in production removes the review and eval gate.

q: A support bot caches a large product-docs system prompt behind one breakpoint and holds a strong cache-read rate for weeks. During a routine release, an engineer unconditionally appends one new tool definition to the request's tool list, gated behind a feature flag that only 5% of traffic can trigger, while the system prompt and message-building code are left untouched. Cache-read tokens then drop to zero on every request, including the 95% that never touch the new tool. What explains the drop?
o: The feature flag itself disables caching for flagged requests regardless of payload content
The cache prefix is rendered as tools, then system, then messages, so any change to the tools array invalidates the cached system and message segments too, not just the tools segment
Adding a tool definition pushes the request past the maximum of four cache breakpoints, so the write silently fails
Tool definitions are excluded from the cacheable prefix entirely, so introducing one always forces a full-price request
e: Correct: the cache is a strict prefix match rendered in the fixed order tools -> system -> messages, and a change at any level invalidates that level plus everything downstream, so an edited tools array busts the system and message caches even though those literal blocks never changed. Option A fails because feature flags are a runtime branch, not a caching input -- the tool entry itself is present in the payload for all 100% of requests regardless of who exercises it. Option C fails because this scenario uses a single breakpoint, well under the limit of four, so the breakpoint cap is not in play. Option D fails because it reverses the real rule: tools sit at the very front of the cacheable hierarchy, not outside it.

q: A data team submits 40,000 documents to the Message Batches API for classification, expecting the batch to finish well inside their six-hour reporting window. To save engineering time, they write the results-processing code to zip the downloaded results directly against the original 40,000-item input list by array position, and they build no handling for a batch that doesn't fully complete. Which two of the following are real risks in this design? (Select two.)
o: Results can return in a different order than requests were submitted, so a positional zip can silently pair a result with the wrong input document
A batch that hasn't finished processing within 24 hours expires, losing whatever requests are still unfinished, so a design with no fallback for that case can silently lose data
The Batches API only applies its cost discount to requests that finish within the first hour, so slower requests are billed at full synchronous price
A single batch submission is capped at 1,000 requests, so the 40,000-document submission would be rejected outright
e: Correct (both): batch requests are processed independently and concurrently, so completion order carries no relationship to submission order -- only a custom_id join is safe, making a positional zip a real data-integrity bug; separately, a batch that has not finished within 24 hours expires and drops unfinished requests, so skipping fallback handling for that case risks silent data loss even though most batches finish in under an hour. Option C fails because the batch discount is a flat percentage off standard pricing applied to all usage in the batch, not a time-boxed promotion tied to how fast a given request completes. Option D fails because the per-batch request ceiling is far larger than 1,000 -- the number is fabricated and would not cause 40,000 documents to be rejected at submission.

q: A platform team pushes a managed-settings.json policy through the claude.ai console that disables one bash command for every engineer at the company. One engineer, annoyed that the command is blocked, adds an explicit allow rule for that same command to their own ~/.claude/settings.json. The command stays blocked when they try to run it. Which explains the behavior?
o: Managed settings sit at the top of the precedence order and override the same key set anywhere below them
User-scope settings always take precedence over any other scope, so the allow rule should have worked
Settings.json changes require a session restart before they take effect, and the restart hasn't happened yet
Command permissions are controlled by CLAUDE.md, not by settings.json, so the allow rule had no effect
e: Managed settings are the highest level in Claude Code's precedence order (managed > command line > project local > shared project > user), so a key set there overrides the same key set at any lower level, including a user's own file. Option 1 inverts the actual order. Option 2 misdiagnoses the cause as timing, but restarting changes nothing since managed still wins after reload. Option 3 confuses CLAUDE.md, which is advisory memory, with settings.json, which is the enforced permission layer that actually governs commands.

q: A team is building a research assistant that runs in Claude Desktop. They want the assistant to always be able to call the company's internal ticket-lookup service in every conversation the user starts on that machine, without the user re-explaining what the service is or how to call it each time they open a new chat. Where should this capability be defined?
o: Restate the ticket-lookup service's API in the first message of every conversation
Add the service description to a claude.ai Project's custom instructions
Connect the ticket-lookup service as an MCP server in Claude Desktop's local configuration
Paste the service's documentation into the system prompt of a single raw API call
e: On Claude Desktop, the instruction surface for tool capability is the connected tooling itself; an MCP server configured locally persists across every conversation on that machine without the user restating anything. Option 0 is the opposite of persistent - it requires re-explaining every time. Option 1 lives in a different product (claude.ai Projects) and would only apply inside that Project's chats, not the Desktop app. Option 3 is scoped to one API call, not a standing capability.

q: A team wants every chat inside a claude.ai Project to follow a house formatting style, and separately wants a guarantee that customer PII never appears in any reply, verified before a response reaches the user, with no exceptions. They plan to write both rules into the Project's custom instructions field.
o: This works for both rules, since Project instructions apply automatically to every chat in the Project
Neither rule belongs in Project instructions, because claude.ai has no persistent instruction surface at all
Only the PII rule belongs in Project instructions; the formatting rule should be a per-chat Style instead
The formatting rule fits there, but a must-never PII guarantee needs enforcement claude.ai's UI configuration can't provide
e: claude.ai Project instructions are UI configuration with no code-level enforcement - fine for a preference like formatting, but a hard guarantee has to be checked deterministically before a response ships, which requires application-level validation or a different interface entirely, not a persuadable instruction. Option 0 wrongly treats both rules as equivalent in kind. Option 1 is false; Project instructions do persist across the Project's chats. Option 2 swaps the two rules' correct treatment backwards.

q: A team is deciding how a multi-step support-ticket application should be structured: whether one Claude call should route escalations to a second, specialized call, or whether a single call should handle each ticket end to end. Which objective actually covers the decision they are making?
o: Claude Application Design, because it concerns Claude's behavior across an application
Agents and Workflows, because this is workflow pattern selection between routing and a single end-to-end call
Claude Application Design, because instruction placement is what determines which pattern gets chosen
Tools and MCPs, because the ticket data has to be retrieved through an external tool
e: Choosing between routing and a single end-to-end call is workflow pattern selection, which sits in Agents and Workflows, not Claude Application Design - the two objectives are explicitly separated. Option 0 is too vague to be the actual tested skill. Option 2 invents a causal relationship that doesn't hold; instruction placement and pattern choice are separate decisions. Option 3 misidentifies the domain based on incidental tool use rather than the structural decision actually being asked about.

q: An internal support application appends each customer's ticket text directly onto the end of the system prompt before sending the request, on the theory that content in the system prompt gets the most attention from the model. The same system prompt template is reused across several thousand tickets per day. A security reviewer flags the design during a routine review. Select the two problems this design actually causes.
o: It collapses the trust boundary between trusted instructions and untrusted ticket content
It reduces the maximum number of output tokens available for the response
It prevents the system prompt prefix from being cached, since the prefix now varies with every ticket
It disables tool use for the remainder of the conversation
e: Appending untrusted ticket text to the system prompt collapses the structural signal that separates instructions from data, and it breaks prompt caching because caching depends on a stable, reused prefix - at several thousand tickets a day that turns into thousands of full-price prefills instead of cache hits. Output token limits and tool availability are governed by separate parameters entirely; neither is affected by what text sits in the prompt prefix.

q: A security team wants a guarantee that no commit ever leaves a repository containing a string matching an API-key pattern, for every engineer, every time, regardless of what any individual session's instructions say. An engineer proposes satisfying this by adding a bullet to the repo's CLAUDE.md telling Claude to check for secrets before committing.
o: This is sufficient, since CLAUDE.md loads automatically in every session for every engineer
This is sufficient as long as the bullet is placed near the top of the file, where the model gives it more weight
This is insufficient; a pre-commit hook that blocks the commit is needed to make the check unconditional
This is insufficient; the rule should instead be duplicated into every engineer's user-scope settings.json
e: CLAUDE.md is advisory text the model reads as guidance, not an enforced control, so it cannot deliver a no-exceptions guarantee; only a hook that runs deterministically on the commit event can block every violating commit regardless of session instructions. Option 0 confuses durability (loads everywhere) with enforcement (isn't optional). Option 1 misconceives how instruction weight works - placement doesn't create a guarantee. Option 3 just duplicates the same advisory text into a policy file's wrong slot without adding any enforcement mechanism.

q: A developer builds a Claude Code plugin containing a skills/ folder with one skill and an agents/ folder with one custom agent, but never creates a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest, assuming the plugin cannot load without one. A teammate installs the plugin locally to test it anyway.
o: The plugin loads; the manifest is optional and Claude Code auto-discovers components from the directory layout
The plugin fails to load entirely; a manifest is required for any plugin to be recognized
Only the skill loads; agents require an explicit manifest entry before they can be discovered
The plugin loads, but only if the folders are renamed to commands/ and hooks/
e: The plugin manifest is optional - when it is absent, Claude Code auto-discovers components straight from the directory layout, including skills/ and agents/, so both the skill and the agent load. Option 1 states a hard requirement that doesn't exist. Option 2 invents an asymmetry between skills and agents that isn't real. Option 3 describes an unnecessary rename; commands/ is an alternate location for skills specifically, not a substitute for agents/, and hooks/ is a different component type altogether.

q: A SaaS analytics vendor's Claude-powered assistant was originally built for one internal team and used a single long-running session that accumulated context across the whole day. Now that the product serves multiple paying customers, engineers notice the assistant sometimes references a different customer's dashboard names in its answers, and they file it as a context-window performance issue to be fixed by summarizing older turns.
o: Correct framing; summarizing the session's earlier turns will resolve the issue
Correct framing; switching to a model with a larger context window will resolve the issue
Incorrect framing; the fix is to remind the assistant at the start of each reply which customer it is currently serving
Incorrect framing; this is a session-isolation requirement, and each customer needs its own session with no shared context
e: Cross-customer leakage is a security boundary failure, not a context-quality problem - the only structural fix is a session per tenant with no shared context. Options 0 and 1 both treat it as something to manage rather than prevent, and neither stops the underlying sharing that causes the leak. Option 2 adds an advisory reminder, which is still just an instruction the model could fail to fully apply, not a boundary that structurally prevents one customer's data from reaching another's session.

q: A platform team distributes an internal plugin through a private marketplace. To signal a new release, they bump the version field in the marketplace catalog entry from 1.2.0 to 1.3.0, but forget that the plugin's own plugin.json manifest still declares version 1.2.0. Team members run the plugin update command afterward.
o: Users receive version 1.3.0, because the marketplace entry takes precedence for signaling new releases
Claude Code throws a version-conflict error and blocks the update until the two files agree
Users keep the cached 1.2.0 build, because Claude Code resolves the version from plugin.json first, silently masking the marketplace entry's value
Claude Code merges the two version strings and installs whichever one is numerically higher
e: Claude Code resolves a plugin's version from its own plugin.json manifest before consulting the marketplace catalog entry, and does so without warning, so a stale manifest version silently masks a version bump made only in the marketplace entry. Assuming the marketplace entry wins gets the precedence backwards. There is no conflict error raised when the two disagree; the mismatch is silent, which is exactly the danger the mechanism creates. There is no merge-and-take-higher behavior either — one field wins outright, and it isn't the marketplace entry.

q: A model an application depends on moves from Active to Deprecated status. Anthropic names a recommended replacement and sets a retirement date roughly 90 days out. The on-call engineer's instinct is to switch the pinned model identifier in every environment, including production, the same day the deprecation notice arrives.
o: Leave the deprecated model pinned everywhere until the retirement date, to avoid any risk of a behavior change before then
Switch every environment, including production, immediately, since deprecated models are already less reliable
Remove the explicit model pin entirely and switch to an alias, so future deprecations are absorbed automatically
Test the replacement model against the existing eval suite first, then roll the pin forward once results clear the bar, well before the retirement date
e: Configuration-management discipline gates any pinned-model change on an eval re-run before promoting it to production, and does so with enough runway before a hard deadline to absorb a failed evaluation. Waiting until the retirement date risks a forced, untested cutover with no time to react if the replacement regresses. Switching immediately without running the eval suite reintroduces exactly the 'quality shifted with no controlled deploy' risk that pinning exists to prevent. Removing the pin in favor of an alias trades one drift problem for a worse one, since an alias updates on Anthropic's schedule rather than on a schedule the team controls.

q: A team lead wants two things guaranteed on every Claude Code invocation across the team, with no reliance on the model choosing to comply: a specific destructive shell command must always be blocked outright, and a formatter script must always run after every file edit. Select the two configuration mechanisms that actually guarantee this behavior regardless of what Claude decides.
o: A CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude never to run that command and to run the formatter after every edit
A permissions.deny rule in the shared, committed project settings.json blocking the command
A PostToolUse hook configured in settings.json that runs the formatter after every file edit
A longer, more detailed instruction appended to every request asking Claude to follow both rules
e: Permission rules and hooks configured in settings.json are enforced by the Claude Code client itself, independent of what the model decides to do on any given turn, which is exactly what 'guaranteed, no exceptions' requires. A CLAUDE.md instruction is delivered as context the model reads and tries to follow, not a control the client enforces, so however clearly it's worded it remains a request rather than a guarantee. Appending a longer instruction to every request has the identical failure mode as the CLAUDE.md option: rewording or relocating a plain-language instruction doesn't change the fact that it's advisory, not deterministic.

q: A data pipeline calls Claude to extract structured fields from support tickets, and the extracted JSON is inserted directly into a downstream Postgres table without any application-level validation. The team currently prompts Claude with 'respond only with JSON matching this schema.' Occasionally a field's type mismatches the column type and the insert fails. Which change most directly prevents malformed JSON from being emitted in the first place?
o: Add a stricter instruction telling Claude to double-check its output before responding
Set output_config.format to a json_schema definition matching the required fields and types
Wrap the insert statement in a try/except block and log failures for manual review
Increase max_tokens so the response is never truncated mid-object
e: output_config.format with a json_schema type uses grammar-constrained decoding, so every generated token is restricted to stay inside the schema — malformed JSON and type mismatches become structurally impossible, not just less likely. A prompt instruction is a soft request the model can still violate. Wrapping the insert in try/except only catches the failure after it happens, it does not prevent the malformed output. Raising max_tokens addresses truncation, not field-type mismatches, which is a different failure mode.

q: A backend service calls an internal REST endpoint to create a customer record, and its client library automatically retries any non-2xx response by resubmitting the same request body. During a traffic spike the endpoint starts returning 409 responses, because an earlier request actually succeeded server-side but its response timed out on the client before arriving, so the client never learned it had already succeeded. What is the correct fix?
o: Increase the client's retry count so the 409 eventually succeeds
Treat 409 as equivalent to 429 and apply the same exponential backoff strategy
Have the client check whether the record already exists before resubmitting the create request, rather than blindly retrying with the same body
Switch the endpoint from REST to GraphQL to avoid status-code ambiguity
e: 409 Conflict means the resource already exists in a state that conflicts with the request; the fix is to inspect current state before acting, not to resend the identical request. Increasing retries just repeats the same failure forever, since the conflict never resolves itself. 429 is a rate-limit signal where backoff helps; 409 is a state-conflict signal where backoff does nothing, so treating them the same is a category error. Swapping protocols doesn't touch the actual bug, which is a missing idempotency check.

q: A nightly reconciliation script kicks off at 1 AM and immediately submits all 900 of the day's transaction records to Claude for anomaly review at once, using asyncio.gather with no concurrency cap. Within the first thirty seconds most requests fail with 429 responses, and the on-call engineer's instinct is to just add a longer fixed delay before each retry. What is the more durable fix?
o: Bound concurrency with a semaphore or queue and ramp the request rate up gradually instead of firing all 900 at once
Keep the current fan-out pattern but add a longer fixed delay before each retry
Switch the reconciliation job to a larger, higher-throughput model so more requests succeed per second
Disable the SDK's built-in retry behavior so failed requests fail fast instead of queuing
e: The root cause is unbounded fan-out, not slow retries — bounding concurrency and ramping traffic gradually is what actually keeps the request rate under the limit. A longer fixed delay treats the symptom on each failed call but the next batch still fires all 900 at once and trips the same limit. Model tier does not change organization-level rate limits, so a larger model doesn't help. Disabling the SDK's own retry/backoff removes a mechanism that was already helping and makes the failure mode worse, not better.

q: A platform team's incident postmortem shows that during a partial Claude API outage, request volume to the API nearly tripled because a wrapper library retried every failed call five times with a fixed one-second delay on top of the official SDK client used underneath it. The wrapper also kept retrying 400 responses caused by a recently introduced malformed-request bug, which never succeeded no matter how many attempts were made. Select the two changes the team should make.
o: Remove the custom wrapper's retry loop and rely on the SDK's built-in max_retries and backoff, which already honors retry-after
Increase the SDK's own max_retries from its default of 2 to a much higher number, in addition to keeping the wrapper
Stop retrying 400-class responses, since they indicate a malformed request that will not succeed regardless of attempts
Add a circuit breaker that halts all traffic to the API for 24 hours after any single failure
e: Removing the redundant wrapper eliminates the double-retry layer that multiplied load during the outage, and the SDK's own max_retries/backoff already honors retry-after. Not retrying 400s is correct because that status is a client error the SDK never retries by default — resending a malformed request cannot succeed. Raising max_retries while keeping the wrapper in place makes the storm worse, since both layers now retry harder. A blanket 24-hour halt is wildly disproportionate to a partial outage and one malformed-request bug, and would take down unrelated, healthy traffic.

q: A senior engineer sees that a teammate's pull request, written entirely by Claude Code, passed the project's automated eval suite and every unit test on the first run. The reviewer is ready to approve it with only a skim, reasoning that a model whose own output already validated cleanly is unlikely to have introduced a subtle bug worth digging for. What should the reviewer do instead?
o: Approve with a skim, since passing evals and unit tests is sufficient signal for AI-authored changes
Apply the same review rigor used for human-written code, regardless of who or what authored it
Ask the same model to regenerate the code a second time and diff the two outputs before deciding
Skip review entirely and rely on the CI pipeline as the sole gate for AI-authored pull requests
e: Provenance doesn't change risk: AI-generated code needs the same review rigor as human-written code, because passing tests and evals only proves the code satisfies what was already checked, not that it's free of subtler issues. Approving on a skim (or skipping review entirely) relaxes the control specifically because of authorship, which is the trap. Regenerating and diffing two outputs from the same model is a superficial consistency check — both generations can share the same blind spot, so it doesn't substitute for actual review.

q: A team's Claude-powered ticket-triage prompt has been hand-edited nine times over two months, each time to fix one specific misclassification, but engineers just paste new wording into the console each time rather than committing it anywhere. When the tenth edit reintroduces a bug that edit six had already fixed, nobody can find what changed between them or why. Which practice addresses the root cause?
o: Increase the prompt's temperature so classification becomes more consistent across edits
Add more few-shot examples to the prompt so the model needs fewer manual edits over time
Switch to a larger model that is less prone to misclassification
Treat the prompt as a versioned artifact — commit each revision to the repository and review changes like code
e: The root cause is that prompt revisions were never checked into source control, so nothing could be diffed, reviewed, or bisected when a regression reappeared. Committing and reviewing prompt changes like code is what makes a reintroduced bug findable and preventable. Temperature, few-shot examples, and a larger model are all prompt-tuning moves that leave the missing versioning process untouched, so the same silent regression can recur regardless of which one is applied.

q: A three-line change to a repository's settings.json disables a permission rule that had been blocking a Claude Code agent from running shell commands as root, and it gets merged straight to main because 'it's just a config tweak, not real code.' Two weeks later the same agent runs an unreviewed destructive command in a teammate's branch. Which practice would most directly have prevented this outcome?
o: Require CLAUDE.md and settings.json changes to go through the same pull-request review and CI gates as source code, since they govern what the system is allowed to do
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent never to run destructive commands
Rotate the API key used by the agent on a monthly schedule
Move the permission setting into a code comment inside CLAUDE.md instead of settings.json
e: settings.json and CLAUDE.md are versioned configuration artifacts that determine what the system is allowed to do, and gating them through the same review and CI pipeline as source code is what would have caught the permission change before merge. A system-prompt instruction is a request the agent can still fail to follow; a permission rule is the deterministic control the prompt instruction can't replace. Key rotation is a credential-hygiene practice unrelated to a permission bypass. Moving the setting into a comment removes its enforcement entirely, making the problem worse.

q: A team asks Claude Code to migrate a 40,000-line billing module from a deprecated ORM to its replacement. Partway through, the agent proposes finishing the whole migration in one sweeping commit that also fixes several unrelated bugs it noticed along the way, reasoning that touching each file only once saves review time. The team is under a hard deadline and finds the one-pass approach tempting. What should they require instead?
o: Approve the single large commit, since touching each file only once reduces total review overhead
Let the agent proceed as proposed, but add a longer QA cycle at the very end to catch any issues
Split the migration into bounded increments with tests passing between each step, and keep the unrelated bug fixes in separate changes
Postpone the migration until after the deadline, since large-scale refactors are inherently too risky to attempt under time pressure
e: The correct discipline for large-scale refactoring is bounded increments with tests green between each step, and never mixing a refactor with a behavior change in the same commit — the unrelated bug fixes are behavior changes and must be split out. Approving the single sweep trades safety for review convenience and mixes concerns. Deferring all verification to one QA pass at the end loses the between-step safety net, making any failure hard to attribute to a specific change. Large-scale refactoring is explicitly in scope and doable under deadline pressure; the fix is incremental discipline, not avoidance.

q: A team wants a repeatable way to describe how they take a Claude-powered feature from initial concept through iterative development, release, and ongoing operation. A vendor pitches a proprietary 'AI Development Lifecycle' framework built specifically for LLM-based projects, arguing that generic IT frameworks predate large language models and can't account for non-deterministic behavior.
o: Adopt the vendor's proprietary AI Development Lifecycle, since generic IT frameworks predate LLM applications
Rely on prompt engineering best practices alone, since they govern how the feature behaves in production
Apply the generic systems life cycle (plan, develop, test, implement, operate, maintain) using Agile or DevOps practices, adding evals as the test gate
Design a new lifecycle framework from scratch, since no existing framework accounts for non-deterministic model output
e: The objective is scoped as generic IT systems life cycle management; Claude-application work maps onto the same plan-develop-test-implement-operate-maintain arc as any other system, with Agile or DevOps supplying the iteration and release discipline and evals replacing exact-match tests as the quality gate. Adopting a proprietary 'AI-specific' framework is the trap this objective is built to catch — an engineered-to-sound-plausible distractor that ignores that the generic model already covers this arc. Prompt engineering is a technique applied during development, not a lifecycle framework in its own right. Building a new framework from scratch overstates the problem: non-determinism is handled by changing what the existing test gate checks, not by discarding the gate.

q: A Claude-powered pipeline is already live in production. An engineer wants to bump the pinned model version and adjust two prompts. Company policy requires a documented change record, a risk assessment, and sign-off from a change advisory board before any modification reaches production, regardless of how small the change is. Which management discipline governs this requirement?
o: Scrum sprint planning, since the change can be scoped and sized as a backlog item
Waterfall requirements sign-off, since the system's original scope must be honored
DevOps continuous deployment, which is designed to automate this kind of approval away
ITIL-style change and release management
e: Documented change records, risk assessment, and change advisory board sign-off before any production modification, no matter how small, is the definition of ITIL-style service management governing a live system. Sprint planning organizes how development work gets scheduled and estimated, not how a change to a live production system gets approved. Waterfall governs how a project's own phases are sequenced during initial build, not ongoing change control after go-live. DevOps automates delivery pipelines, but 'automates approval away' directly contradicts the stem's explicit requirement for a human sign-off — a distractor that sounds efficient while ignoring the stated constraint.

q: A telehealth company routes post-visit session summaries through Claude for clinician review. A newly passed data protection law in the patient's home country prohibits any processing of health data outside that country's borders, even momentarily in transit. Which infrastructure requirement should the solution architecture satisfy?
o: Encrypt the session summary with a customer-managed key before it leaves the clinic's network
Route the request through a regional API endpoint that guarantees in-country processing
Shorten the retention window on stored session summaries to reduce exposure
Increase the request timeout budget to accommodate cross-border network latency
e: The constraint is where processing happens, not how long data is kept or how fast a response arrives. A regional endpoint pins inference to the required jurisdiction. Encryption protects confidentiality in transit but doesn't control the country in which the model actually runs, so it fails the residency requirement outright. Shortening retention addresses how long data is stored, a different requirement dimension than where it's processed. Increasing the timeout is a latency parameter with no bearing on jurisdiction.

q: A brokerage firm's policy states that every response Claude sends to a retail customer must have account numbers stripped before delivery, with no exceptions permitted under any circumstance. A junior engineer proposes solving this by adding a instruction to the system prompt asking Claude to redact account numbers whenever it sees one. What does this requirement actually call for?
o: A longer, more detailed system prompt describing exactly what an account number looks like
A higher reasoning-effort configuration on the model to improve redaction accuracy
Periodic manual audits of a sample of outgoing customer responses
A deterministic post-processing filter that runs on every response before delivery, independent of model behavior
e: "No exceptions permitted under any circumstance" means the requirement demands a guarantee, and a guarantee requires a deterministic control that runs regardless of what the model decides. A prompt instruction, however detailed, is still a request the model tries to follow, not a guarantee, so option 0 fails on the same grounds as the junior engineer's original proposal. Higher reasoning effort can reduce error rates but never eliminates them, so it can't satisfy "no exceptions." Sampled manual audits catch problems after some have already reached customers, which directly contradicts a zero-exception requirement.

q: A project brief for an HR tool reads: 'Claude should draft a personalized onboarding email for each new hire based on their role and start date.' The same brief adds that the tool must stay responsive with sub-second turnaround even when 200 new hires start on the same day. A requirements analyst is sorting these two statements into a functional requirements document and an infrastructure requirements document.
o: Both statements belong in infrastructure requirements, since they both describe system behavior under real operating conditions
Both statements belong in functional requirements, since neither one names a specific vendor or region
The email-drafting behavior is functional; the sub-second-at-200-concurrent-hires statement is infrastructure
The latency statement is functional, since it directly shapes what the end user experiences
e: Functional requirements describe what the system does (draft a personalized email); infrastructure requirements describe the non-functional envelope it must operate within (a throughput and latency constraint under concurrent load). Calling both statements infrastructure ignores that drafting the email is itself the capability being built, not a constraint on it. Calling both functional, on the reasoning that neither names a vendor or region, misses that a capacity/performance ceiling is the textbook definition of an infrastructure requirement regardless of vendor mention. Labeling the latency statement functional conflates user-experienced quality with the feature itself — latency-under-load is a quality attribute, not a capability.
